books.section: Topic 2.5 Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans

primary_sources: Mary Rowlandson, Narrative of the Captivity and Restoration (1682)

parts.modelAnswer: Rowlandson describes the attackers as “hell-hounds” and as wolves tearing sheep — as cruel, godless enemies rather than as human beings. Her language turns the attackers into agents of evil, not people with their own reasons for fighting.
parts.prompt: Identify one way Rowlandson describes the Native peoples who attacked Lancaster.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for naming one accurate feature of Rowlandson's description, such as calling the attackers hell-hounds or wolves, or describing them as cruel and godless.
scoring.notEarned: Naming only that Rowlandson was attacked, with no feature of her description, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: Rowlandson wrote as a grieving captive who had just watched her neighbors killed and her daughter wounded, so her account is shaped by trauma and fear. She also wrote for a Puritan audience that expected her suffering to prove God's providence, so she cast the war as a struggle between Christians and heathens.
parts.prompt: Explain one way Rowlandson's situation as a captive shaped the way she wrote about Native peoples.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one accurate way her situation shaped her writing, such as trauma and grief from the attack, her position as a captive, or her Puritan audience's expectation of a providential story.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that Rowlandson disliked Native peoples, with no link to her situation as a captive, does not earn the point.

parts.modelAnswer: One consequence was the destruction of Native power in New England: Metacom was killed in August 1676, and many survivors were sold into slavery in the West Indies. The war ended organized Native resistance in southern New England and cleared the way for English expansion.
parts.prompt: Explain one consequence of King Philip's War for Native peoples in New England.

scoring.criterion: Earns the point for explaining one accurate consequence, such as the death of Metacom, the enslavement of survivors, the end of organized Native resistance, or the opening of New England to English expansion.
scoring.notEarned: Stating only that many people died in the war, with no consequence for Native peoples explained, does not earn the point.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim quotation from Mary Rowlandson, Narrative of the Captivity and Restoration (1682), public domain

stimulus.source_note: Mary Rowlandson, Narrative of the Captivity and Restoration (1682), describing the attack on Lancaster, Massachusetts, in February 1676. Public domain.
stimulus.text: It is a solemn sight to see so many Christians lying in their blood, some here, and some there, like a company of sheep torn by wolves, all of them stripped naked by a company of hell-hounds, roaring, singing, ranting, and insulting, as if they would have torn our very hearts out; yet the Lord by His almighty power preserved a number of us from death, for there were twenty-four of us taken alive and carried captive.
